steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper presenting SLiMe (Segment Like Me), a one-shot segmentation method built on Stable Diffusion that segments objects or parts at any granularity from a single annotated example. Motivate the problem, review related zero-shot and few-shot methods, and summarize the approach and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Segmentation at different granularities; what end-users need
- Related work: zero-shot, text-based and few-shot segmentation and their limits
- One-shot learning with SegGPT and its data requirement
- SLiMe: idea and two key insights
- How SLiMe works and summary of results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Granularity and user needs
  - segmentation is multifaceted, solutions at various granularity levels
  - expression recognition / facial alignment: basic regions (nose, eyes) may suffice
  - visual effects (wrinkle removal): finer segments like eye bags, forehead, chin
  - end-user: say what to segment and level of detail over many images with one or a few segmented examples used for training
  - user shouldn't have to curate a big dataset with masks, train a big model, or encode elaborate object properties
  - -> customizable, few-sample, granularity-adaptive, intuitive to define/refine: high importance
- Related work
  - recent research on lack of segmentation data: zero-shot, text-description based, few-shot
  - DiffSeg: zero-shot, based on SD, segments everything; not controllable (which object, granularity) -> can't segment a specific object/part given a train sample
  - Peekaboo: textual description; with SD and its loss optimizes a randomly initialized mask; text description unique per image, not transferrable -> can't segment test images from train images
  - ReGAN: trains a GAN on data of a specific class, generates data, user manually annotates, GAN features + annotations train a segmentation model
  - SegDDPM: features from a pre-trained diffusion model (DM), ensemble of MLPs, few labeled data
  - both good with 10-50 examples, struggle with extremely limited samples; need training on category-specific data (e.g. a large dataset of horse images, cumbersome)
- SegGPT
  - one-shot learning; trained on color-randomized segmentation data (instance + part-level masks)
  - inference: segments only one region of a target image from a reference image + binary mask
  - effective, but needs a lot of annotated data for initial training -> training with a single annotation still unaddressed
- SLiMe
  - segments any object/part from the same category given one image + its mask, arbitrary granularity, one-shot (Figure 1, Figure 8)
  - avoids extensive annotated data or training a GAN per class
  - leverages Stable Diffusion (SD), large-scale pre-trained vision/language model
  - recent studies: SD cross-attention maps highlight different image regions as text changes; used to modify generated images and for image correspondence
  - insight 1: one-shot optimization, fine-tune SD text embeddings to capture segmented regions from reference image + mask; one text embedding per region
  - insight 2: standalone cross-attention maps -> imprecise segmentations (Figure 2); propose weighted accumulated self (WAS)-attention map (Section 4): semantic boundary info, higher-resolution self-attention maps
- Method and results
  - single image + mask fine-tune SD text embeddings via cross- and WAS-attention maps
  - refined embeddings emphasize segmented regions; used at inference on real-world images, same granularity
  - quantitative + qualitative experiments
  - with one or a handful of examples: better than or comparable to supervised methods needing extensive training
  - no category-specific training, still beats other few-shot techniques on average and most parts, almost all datasets
  - 10-sample: ReGAN by nearly 10\%, SegDDPM by about 2\%
  - 1-sample: SegGPT by around 12\%, SegDDPM by nearly 11\%

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Image segmentation is a problem with many facets, and solutions exist at various levels of granularity. For example, in applications like expression recognition or facial alignment, it might be enough to segment images of faces into basic regions like nose and eyes. But in visual effects applications, more detailed segments like eye bags, forehead and chin are needed for tasks like wrinkle removal. Also, from the point of view of an end-user, a simple and effective way to guide a segmentation method is to decide what to segment and the level of detail wanted across a broad set of images by giving only one or a few segmented examples for the method to train on. At the same time the user should not have to curate a large dataset with segmentation masks, train a large segmentation model, or encode elaborate and specific properties of the target objects into the model. So a customizable segmentation method that can adapt to different levels of granularity using a few annotated samples, and that lets users intuitively define and refine the target segmentation for their specific requirements, is very important.

Recent research has tackled the lack of segmentation data by looking into zero-shot segmentation, segmentation based on textual descriptions, and few-shot learning. DiffSeg is a zero-shot segmentation method based on SD, and it segments everything in the image. However DiffSeg cannot be used to segment a specific object or part in the test images given a train sample, because its segmentation is not controllable in terms of which object to segment and the segmentation granularity. Peekaboo is another work, which uses a textual description for segmentation. Given an image and a textual description of the target object, they use Stable Diffusion and its loss function to optimize a randomly initialized segmentation mask until it reaches the desired mask. But it cannot be used to segment test images given train images, because the textual description of the target object is unique in each image and is not transferrable. Another promising method is ReGAN. ReGAN first trains a GAN on the data of the specific class they want to segment. After that they generate data with this GAN and the user manually annotates the generated data. Then the features of the generated data from the GAN and the annotations are both used to train a segmentation model. SegDDPM on the other hand extracts features from a pre-trained diffusion model (DM) and trains an ensemble of MLPs for segmentation using few labeled data. Both are very good at segmentation with 10-50 examples but they struggle when there are extremely limited samples. Also these models need training on data specific to each category. For example, to segment horses you need to collect a large dataset of horse images, which can be a cumbersome task.

SegGPT, on the other hand, uses one-shot learning, and it is trained on color-randomized segmentation data that includes both instance and part-level masks. At inference it segments only one region in a target image, using a reference image and its binary segmentation mask. SegGPT is effective, but it needs a large amount of annotated segmentation data for the initial training, so the challenge of training effectively with a single annotation is still not addressed.

- SLiMe
  - segments any object/part from the same category given one image + its mask, arbitrary granularity, one-shot (Figure 1, Figure 8); no extensive annotated data, no GAN per class
  - leverages Stable Diffusion (SD), large-scale pre-trained vision/language model
  - recent studies: SD cross-attention maps highlight different regions as text changes; used to modify generated images and for image correspondence
  - insight 1: one-shot optimization, fine-tune SD text embeddings per segmented region, guided by reference image + mask
  - insight 2: standalone cross-attention maps imprecise (Figure 2) -> weighted accumulated self (WAS)-attention map (Section 4), boundary info + higher-resolution self-attention
- Method and results
  - single image + mask fine-tune SD text embeddings via cross- and WAS-attention maps; used at inference, same granularity
  - one or a handful of examples: better than or comparable to supervised methods
  - beats other few-shot techniques on average and most parts, almost all datasets
  - 10-sample: ReGAN nearly 10\%, SegDDPM about 2\%; 1-sample: SegGPT around 12\%, SegDDPM nearly 11\%

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Image segmentation is a problem with many facets, and solutions exist at various levels of granularity. For example, in applications like expression recognition or facial alignment, it might be enough to segment images of faces into basic regions like nose and eyes. So a customizable segmentation method that can adapt to different levels of granularity using a few annotated samples, and that lets users intuitively define and refine the target segmentation for their specific requirements, is very important.

However DiffSeg cannot be used to segment a specific object or part in the test images given a train sample, because its segmentation is not controllable in terms of which object to segment and the segmentation granularity. Peekaboo is another work, which uses a textual description for segmentation. Given an image and a textual description of the target object, they use Stable Diffusion and its loss function to optimize a randomly initialized segmentation mask until it reaches the desired mask. But it cannot be used to segment test images given train images, because the textual description of the target object is unique in each image and is not transferrable. Another promising method is ReGAN. ReGAN first trains a GAN on the data of the specific class they want to segment. After that they generate data with this GAN and the user manually annotates the generated data. Then the features of the generated data from the GAN and the annotations are both used to train a segmentation model. SegDDPM on the other hand extracts features from a pre-trained diffusion model (DM) and trains an ensemble of MLPs for segmentation using few labeled data. Both are very good at segmentation with 10-50 examples but they struggle when there are extremely limited samples. Also these models need training on data specific to each category. For example, to segment horses you need to collect a large dataset of horse images, which can be a cumbersome task.

SegGPT, on the other hand, uses one-shot learning, and it is trained on color-randomized segmentation data that includes both instance and part-level masks. At inference it segments only one region in a target image, using a reference image and its binary segmentation mask. SegGPT is effective, but it needs a large amount of annotated segmentation data for the initial training, so the challenge of training effectively with a single annotation is still not addressed.

In this paper we propose Segment Like Me (SLiMe), which segments any object or part from the same category based on a given image and its segmentation mask, with an arbitrary granularity level and in a one-shot way, so there is no need for extensive annotated segmentation data or for training a generative model like a GAN for a specific class (see Figure 1 and Figure 8 for some examples). To do this we use the rich knowledge of an existing large-scale pre-trained vision/language model, Stable Diffusion (SD). Recent studies have shown that the cross-attention maps of models like SD highlight different regions of the image when the corresponding text changes. This property has been used to modify generated images and to get image correspondence. Building on this idea, we have two key insights. The first is that the multifaceted segmentation problem can be framed as a one-shot optimization task where we fine-tune the text embeddings of SD to capture semantic details like segmented regions, guided by a reference image and its segmentation mask, and each text embedding corresponds to a distinct segmented region. The second is that we observed that using standalone cross-attention maps leads to imprecise segmentations, as shown in Figure 2. To fix this we propose a new weighted accumulated self (WAS)-attention map (see Section 4). This attention map incorporates important semantic boundary information and uses higher-resolution self-attention maps, which makes the segmentation more accurate.

Based on these insights, SLiMe uses a single image and its segmentation mask to fine-tune the text embeddings of SD through cross- and WAS-attention maps. These refined embeddings emphasize the segmented regions in these attention maps, and they are used to segment real-world images at inference, with the same granularity as the segmented region in the image that was used for optimization. We show the efficacy of our approach with various quantitative and qualitative experiments. Even when it relies on just one or a handful of examples, SLiMe is better than or comparable to supervised counterparts that need extensive training. Also, even though it is not trained on a specific category, SLiMe outperforms other few-shot techniques on average and on most parts, across almost all the datasets. For example we outperform ReGAN by nearly 10\% and SegDDPM by about 2\% in a 10-sample setting. And in a 1-sample setting we beat SegGPT by around 12\% and SegDDPM by nearly 11\%.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Image segmentation is a multifaceted problem, with solutions existing at various levels of granularity. For instance, in applications like expression recognition or facial alignment, segmenting images of faces into basic regions like nose and eyes might suffice. However, in visual effects applications, more detailed segments such as eye bags, forehead, and chin are necessary for tasks like wrinkle removal. Moreover, from the perspective of an end-user, a straightforward and effective way to guide a segmentation method is to determine what to segment and the desired level of detail across a broad set of images by providing only one or a few segmented examples for the method to use for training. Meanwhile, the user should not need to curate a large dataset with segmentation masks, train a large segmentation model, or encode elaborate and specific properties of target objects into the model. As a result, a customizable segmentation method that can adapt to different levels of granularity using a few annotated samples, and that lets users intuitively define and refine the target segmentation according to their specific requirements, is of high importance.

Recent research has tackled the lack of segmentation data by delving into zero-shot, textual description based segmentation, and few-shot learning. DiffSeg [1] is a zero-shot segmentation method based on SD, which segments everything in the image. However, DiffSeg cannot be used to segment a specific object or part in the test images given a train sample, because its segmentation is not controllable in terms of which object to segment and the segmentation granularity. Peekaboo [2] is another work, which uses textual description for segmentation. Given an image and a textual description of the target object to be segmented, they use Stable Diffusion and its loss function to optimize a randomly initialized segmentation mask to reach the desired mask. Nevertheless, it cannot be used to segment test images given train images, because the textual description of the target object in each image is unique and not transferrable. Another promising method is ReGAN [3]. ReGAN first trains a GAN [4] on the data of a specific class they aim to segment. They then generate data with this GAN, and the user manually annotates the generated data. Both the generated data's features from the GAN and the annotations are then used to train a segmentation model. In contrast, SegDDPM [5] extracts features from a pre-trained diffusion model (DM) and trains an ensemble of MLPs for segmentation using few labeled data. Both excel in segmentation with 10-50 examples but struggle with extremely limited samples. Furthermore, these models require training on data specific to each category. For instance, to segment horses, one has to collect a large dataset of horse images, a task that can be cumbersome.

SegGPT [6], in turn, employs one-shot learning, training on color-randomized segmentation data which includes both instance and part-level masks. During inference, it segments only one region in a target image using a reference image and its binary segmentation mask. While SegGPT is effective, it demands a significant amount of annotated segmentation data for initial training, leaving the challenge of training effectively with a single annotation unaddressed.

In this paper, we propose Segment Like Me (SLiMe), which segments any object/part from the same category based on a given image and its segmentation mask, with an arbitrary granularity level and in a one-shot manner, avoiding the need for extensive annotated segmentation data or for training a generative model like a GAN for a specific class (see Figure 1 and Figure 8 for some examples). For this purpose, we leverage the rich knowledge of an existing large-scale pre-trained vision/language model, Stable Diffusion (SD) [7]. Recent studies like [8] have shown that the cross-attention maps of models like SD highlight different regions of the image when the corresponding text changes. This property has been used to modify generated images [8] and to achieve image correspondence [9]. Expanding on this idea, we present two key insights. First, the multifaceted segmentation problem can be framed as a one-shot optimization task in which we fine-tune the text embeddings of SD to capture semantic details such as segmented regions, guided by a reference image and its segmentation mask, where each text embedding corresponds to a distinct segmented region. Second, we observed that using standalone cross-attention maps leads to imprecise segmentations, as shown in Figure 2. To rectify this, we propose a novel weighted accumulated self (WAS)-attention map (see Section 4). This attention map incorporates crucial semantic boundary information and uses higher-resolution self-attention maps, improving segmentation accuracy.

Based on these insights, SLiMe uses a single image and its segmentation mask to fine-tune SD's text embeddings through cross- and WAS-attention maps. These refined embeddings emphasize the segmented regions within these attention maps, and are used to segment real-world images during inference, mirroring the granularity of the segmented region in the image used for optimization. Through various quantitative and qualitative experiments, we show the efficacy of our approach. SLiMe, even when relying on just one or a handful of examples, proves to be better than or comparable to supervised counterparts that demand extensive training. Furthermore, despite not being trained on a specific category, SLiMe outperforms other few-shot techniques on average and on most parts, across almost all the datasets. For instance, we outperform ReGAN [3] by nearly 10\% and SegDDPM [5] by approximately 2\% in a 10-sample setting. Additionally, in a 1-sample setting, we exceed SegGPT by around 12\% and SegDDPM by nearly 11\%.
